kp.k: Shared foundation models connect legal change to broader markets
kp.d: Abramowitz argues that legal AI differs from earlier industry-specific technology revolutions because industries now use the same underlying models. He recommends following broader market developments to understand their legal manifestations, rather than treating legal technology as an isolated market.
qs: Today, since we’re all working off the same basic group of models, the AI that legal has—is the AI that accounting has—is the AI that manufacturing has—we’re all working with those same tools.
If you follow the whole market, you can see more clearly where legal is going.

kp.k: 2026 shifts attention toward agents and measurable business impact
kp.d: Abramowitz predicts a transition from AI assistants in 2025 to agents in 2026, alongside a shift from awareness and adoption measures toward ROI, profit margins, pricing and service design. These are his forecasts, not reported measurements of achieved legal-market outcomes.
qs: AI assistants were the key tool of 2025. In 2026, you’re really going to hear more about AI agents.
But I think in 2026, we’re not going to be looking at adoption anymore. We’re going to be measuring impact. We’re going to start measuring ROI.
How does it show up in pricing and service design?

kp.k: Usage metrics may miss AI's enduring cognitive benefits
kp.d: Drawing on his own experience, Abramowitz says AI supports confidence and changes how he approaches problems even when he does not actively consult it. He cautions that reduced time using AI need not indicate reduced usefulness and describes learning when not to use it, including preferring human-written emails.
qs: I think AI can be very useful even if you use it more sporadically.
As our brains evolve and we begin to think differently, we’re going to find that there are certain places where we don’t need it anymore because our starting point is so much higher.

kp.k: Coding advances illustrate reduced delegation and broader individual responsibility
kp.d: Abramowitz presents Wix.com's acquisition of Base44 as a cross-domain signal more important than legal-AI funding rounds. He describes the purchase as $80 million, less than 10% of Wix's market capitalization, and Base44 as essentially run by one technical person. He connects AI coding to Wix's proposed end-to-end 'X engineer' role; this is a software-work analogy, not evidence of a corresponding legal staffing change.
qs: And for $80 million, less than 10% of our market cap, we can buy a company that is going to be our lifeline into the future.
What they bought with Base44 was a company that had been run essentially by a single person who had coded everything.

There’s a concept now at Wix being developed called the “X engineer.” And the idea is you’re no longer a DevOps or a frontend or a backend engineer. You are doing everything. You’re responsible for the feature end to end.

kp.k: Bespoke legal work could encourage lawyer-built applications
kp.d: Abramowitz reports seeing lawyers share AI-built applications, including a Hong Kong lawyer attempting to replicate Harvey and other vendors' features using Google AI Studio. He predicts more lawyer and law-firm 'vibe coding,' especially at the edges of legal work where existing products lack customization. He treats bespoke work as a reason to build tailored tools, while warning that build-versus-buy deliberation can prevent action.
qs: There’s a lawyer in Hong Kong who’s gone on LinkedIn using Google AI Studio to try to replicate features in Harvey and other big legal tech companies. And it’s working.
But if I can take Claude Code and build something very specific around what we do and how we work, that might be more effective.
But I do think you’re going to see a lot more lawyers and law firms vibe coding solutions—especially at the fringes or edges of legal work.

kp.k: Accumulated AI experience may widen professional divides
kp.d: Abramowitz predicts a widening gap in 2026 between users and non-users because learning involves an accumulated mindset rather than merely operating software. He recommends starting now rather than waiting for better tools. Leonard separately describes intelligent peers resisting AI for ethical, security and humanity-related reasons, acknowledging legitimate concerns rather than treating all hesitation as technical ignorance.
qs: I think this is one of the themes of 2026 — you’re going to start to see a widening divide between those who have been using AI and those who haven’t.
Wrapping your brain around AI has compounding interest. It’s not something you develop in a day.
That’s why I’ve told lawyers from the beginning: just start using this.
So it’s confusing when you’re trying to help other people understand — especially because there are legitimate concerns people have.

kp.k: Reported surveys connect usage, sentiment and organizational scale
kp.d: Abramowitz cites a Law360 survey from the preceding year as showing more positive AI sentiment among heavier users and a recent Wharton study as finding that smaller companies can better measure AI impact and ROI. The transcript supplies no sample sizes, methods or numerical results, so these remain his summaries of external research. His accompanying comparison of small revenue-generating startups with larger organizations is qualitative.
qs: The Law360 survey showed this beautifully last year — positive sentiment toward AI increases the more you use it. The people who like it the least are those who haven’t used it.
There was a Wharton study recently that showed the smaller your company is, the more you’re able to measure the impact and ROI of AI.

kp.k: Founder quality attracts venture investment into legal AI
kp.d: Abramowitz estimates that legal-tech startups number in the thousands, contrasting with Leonard's recollection of 400–500 on a LegalTech Hub poster. He reports Jonathan Levy's explanation that Y Combinator is investing in more legal-tech companies because more 'top 1%' founders are entering the field, not because it has adopted a sector preference. Abramowitz interprets investment as following entrepreneurs' expectations of building major companies in legal.
qs: I think it’s actually in the thousands at this point.
And he said, no, we’re investing in more legal tech companies, but we’re totally vertical agnostic. It’s just that there are more top 1% founders building companies in the legal space right now.
It’s not because investors suddenly love legal. It’s because entrepreneurs see legal as a place where they can build generational companies.

kp.k: AI targets reasoning shortages rather than information storage
kp.d: Abramowitz argues that legal services face high demand and constrained supplies of intelligence and reasoning, making AI more valuable than earlier database-oriented software. He uses TrialKit, which he says sells mostly to criminal defense attorneys, and its founder's report of limited previous technology purchasing as illustrations. He identifies understaffed defense practices and courts as needing reasoning capacity and predicts that apparently excessive startup valuations may eventually look low; no quantified service or court outcomes are supplied.
qs: And I think the reason that’s true is that legal often has high demand and sometimes low supply of intelligence and reasoning.
Take a company like TrialKit, which sells mostly to criminal defense attorneys.
The courts do not have enough intelligence and reasoning capacity to function the way they need to — to make the trains keep running.
And I think we’ll look back and say those valuations were actually fairly low for the amount of value being created.

kp.k: Cheaper software development threatens startup moats and financing models
kp.d: Despite his optimism about legal AI's value, Abramowitz says he stopped investing in startups when ChatGPT launched because defensibility became uncertain. He questions whether cheaper AI-assisted development and smaller teams reduce the need for venture financing and describes competition from foundation-model providers as a structural investment risk. These are concerns and possibilities, not a finding that venture capital has become obsolete.
qs: Now, at the same time, I stopped investing in startups when ChatGPT launched. Because my concern was: what’s the moat anymore? Can anyone do this?

The idea of investing a huge amount of money to build a software company — with vibe coding and everything we just talked about — the cost of developing software and the need to staff with big teams is just not what it used to be.
Do you really need venture capital financing to build and scale companies? I think that’s a legitimate question.

kp.k: Law-firm adoption produces uneven results and service redesign pressures
kp.d: Abramowitz reports mixed law-firm experiences: some have successfully deployed personal assistants and are considering how to improve client prices, turnaround and communication; others are cancelling subscriptions or have experienced ineffective training. These are consultancy observations without identified firms or quantified outcomes. He frames client-facing service improvement as the next challenge beyond individual adoption.
qs: We got our folks onto a personal AI assistant. Now we have to figure out how we’re actually going to make this work so that the client isn’t paying as much, or isn’t waiting as long to get their work back, or is being kept more updated — so that the service is better.
And I can tell you there are other firms where they’re canceling subscriptions because it felt like it didn’t work.
There are firms that have had a heck of a time with training, and the way they did the training just absolutely didn’t take.

kp.k: AI-first competitors intensify pressure on established law firms
kp.d: Abramowitz says incumbent leaders respond more strongly to AI-first firms than to familiar vendor demonstrations. He describes lawyers leaving to compete with former firms using existing tools rather than large venture rounds or major R&D investment. He predicts competitive threats will sustain investment despite uneven adoption, while explicitly leaving open whether AI-first entrants or better-executing traditional firms will prevail.
qs: At the same time, the AI-first firm is probably the scariest thing law firm leaders have seen.
the tools that exist today, out of the box, effectively enable me to start a firm that competes directly with my old firm
Whether that threat ends up being AI-first firms or traditional firms that execute better — that remains to be seen.

kp.k: AI investment may reopen external ownership and financing debates
kp.d: Leonard reports that private equity's potential to capture AI benefits alarms firm leaders. Abramowitz predicts renewed debate in 2026 about external nonlawyer ownership and financing, arguing that firms must fund both AI and talent retention against competitors such as Kirkland, Latham and Paul Weiss. He reports conference discussion in late 2025 about whether McDermott Will & Schulte's chairman was suggesting an MSO and external financing, not a confirmed transaction. He says external financing is already appearing in personal injury and AI-first firms but qualifies its applicability at Big Law scale.
qs: In 2026, we’re going to revisit the concept of external non-lawyer ownership in law firms.
It’s that they feel like they can’t only invest in AI. They have to invest in talent as well.
It remains to be seen whether it works at Big Law scale.
It was whether the chairman of McDermott Will & Schulte was suggesting that the firm might create an MSO and take in external financing.

kp.k: AGI is framed as continuing adaptation, not sudden replacement
kp.d: Asked by McCormack about competing AGI timelines and a possible one-to-two-year horizon, Abramowitz does not endorse a specific timeline. He views AGI definitions as moving goalposts, identifies ChatGPT 3.5's release as the decisive advance and predicts that people will develop new activities as AI raises capabilities. Podcasting and earning money through dancing on camera serve as analogies for emergent work; his statement that he is not working less is personal experience, not labor-market evidence.
qs: I think the very existence of the term “AGI” reflects a constant moving of the goalposts when it comes to AI.
To say AGI is the moment when humans get replaced — I don’t see it that way.
By the time we get to whatever point people are calling AGI — whether that’s five years from now or sooner — the human brain will have adjusted, and there will be new things we do.
I’ve been using AI for three years. I’m not working less.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Zach Abramowitz predicts a shift toward agents and measurable business impact, more lawyer-built software, widening differences between adopters and non-adopters, and competitive and financing changes in legal markets.
pts.d:
1. Measurement and tools: Abramowitz characterizes 2024 as focused on awareness and 2025 as the year of pronounced workplace adoption and AI assistants. He predicts that 2026 will emphasize agents and measurable impact on ROI, margins, pricing and service design rather than adoption or subjective productivity alone. He also expects rapid developments to make feeling behind increasingly normal.

2. Custom legal applications: He reports that lawyers are already building applications and replicating features of commercial legal-AI products. He predicts more lawyers and firms will use vibe coding to build customized solutions, particularly at the edges of legal work that existing applications do not handle out of the box. In his account, bespoke work is a reason for this development, not a barrier to it.

3. Compounding adoption advantage: He predicts a widening divide between AI users and non-users because developing an AI-oriented mindset takes time and compounds with experience. He also argues that lower usage time need not indicate lower usefulness: AI can improve users' starting points and confidence even when they do not actively consult it. This is an experiential claim, not a measured productivity result.

4. Startup opportunity and vulnerability: He attributes increased legal-tech investment to talented founders entering a market with high demand and constrained supplies of intelligence and reasoning. He argues that AI supplies something more valuable than earlier database-oriented software and predicts that apparently high startup valuations may eventually look low relative to value created. Simultaneously, he questions startup defensibility and whether AI-assisted software development reduces the need for large teams and venture financing. He explicitly treats competition from foundation-model providers as a structural risk.

5. Uneven incumbent adoption and service redesign: He reports mixed law-firm results: some firms have achieved traction and are considering how to improve prices, turnaround and client updates, while others are cancelling subscriptions or struggling with training. These service improvements are described as the next implementation challenge, not as established sector-wide outcomes.

6. Competitive pressure: He argues that existing off-the-shelf tools enable departing lawyers to establish AI-first firms competing with their former employers without massive fundraising or R&D. He predicts that threats from AI-first entrants, or better-executing traditional firms, will keep incumbents investing despite mixed adoption results. He does not settle which type of competitor will ultimately prevail.

7. External financing: He predicts renewed discussion in 2026 of external non-lawyer ownership and financing. Firms' simultaneous need to fund AI and retain expensive talent makes external capital attractive. He says external financing is already appearing in personal injury and AI-first firms, but leaves its viability at Big Law scale unresolved.

8. Work and AGI: He rejects treating AGI as a single moment when humans are replaced. Instead, he predicts continuing adjustment to higher AI-enabled starting points and the emergence of new human activities. He does not provide a specific forecast for lawyer employment or endorse an AGI arrival date.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Abramowitz primarily supports his claims with personal use, advisory experience, reported conversations and examples; he also cites two studies without supplying their methods or numerical results.
pts.d:
For the transition from awareness to adoption to impact, Abramowitz refers broadly to surveys from 2024–2025 without naming instruments or reporting figures. His reasoning also uses a cross-industry premise: legal, accounting and manufacturing work from the same underlying model families, so broader market developments can signal legal changes.

For custom software and reduced development staffing, he invokes Wix's acquisition of Base44, which he describes as an $80 million purchase of a business essentially built by one technical founder, and the emerging end-to-end 'X engineer' role at Wix. These are software-industry examples supporting his legal-market extrapolation, not measurements of legal productivity. He reports observing a Hong Kong lawyer using Google AI Studio to replicate features of Harvey and other products, followed by other lawyers posting their own applications. No independent performance or reliability assessment is supplied.

For mindset and adoption differences, he draws on his own three years of use and conversations with lawyers. He reports that a Law360 survey from the preceding year found more positive sentiment among more frequent users. He also reports that a recent Wharton study found smaller companies better able to measure AI impact and ROI. The transcript supplies neither sample details nor effect sizes; these references do not establish a causal benefit of use or greater realized ROI in small firms.

For startup investment, he recounts a conversation with Y Combinator's Jonathan Levy about stronger founders entering legal. This is reported authority used to support Abramowitz's own explanation, not independent investment-flow data. He uses TrialKit's criminal-defense market and its founder's account of historically sparse technology purchasing as an example of unmet demand for reasoning assistance. His own decision to stop startup investing when ChatGPT launched illustrates his concerns about moats and financing, rather than proving those risks will materialize.

For incumbent adoption and competitive threats, he relies on advisory observations of firms, training failures, subscription cancellations and leadership reactions to AI-first competitors. No firms, counts or service outcome measurements are provided for those observations. For external financing, he cites conversations with firms and private-equity participants, plus discussion at a late-2025 legal innovators conference about whether McDermott Will & Schulte might establish an MSO and take external financing. That example is presented as discussion of a possibility, not a completed transaction.

For human adaptation, he offers historical analogies involving podcasting and earning money through online performance, and notes that he personally is not working less. These support his argument by analogy and experience rather than a legal labor-market forecast.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The principal forecast horizon is 2026, while startup valuations, financing disruption and human adaptation are longer-term claims without firm deadlines.
pts.d:
The interview is situated at the start of 2026. Abramowitz explicitly places the shift toward agents, ROI measurement, a widening user/non-user divide and renewed ownership discussions in that year. Lawyer-built applications are described as an observable development over the preceding few months, with further growth anticipated but no adoption target or completion date.

Custom application development is conditional on commercial products being insufficiently customizable and tools such as Claude Code enabling more specific solutions. He cautions that build-versus-buy deliberation can produce paralysis. The adoption advantage depends on sustained experimentation and developing a mindset, not merely learning interface functions; he offers no quantified catch-up period.

Startup value predictions are retrospective-looking forecasts expressed as what people will eventually recognize. They are qualified by uncertain defensibility, cheaper software development and the risk that major model providers absorb startup functions. His question about the venture-capital model is a stated concern, not a claim that it has already disappeared.

Incumbent competition is near-term and based on tools available 'today,' but Abramowitz leaves open whether AI-first entrants or more effective traditional firms will pose the decisive threat. External financing is framed as an emerging response to competing AI and talent budgets, with Big Law scalability explicitly uncertain. His AGI discussion does not accept the host's suggested one-to-two-year horizon; he refers to five years or sooner only illustratively and predicts adaptation rather than a discrete replacement event.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed effects span individual lawyers, incumbent and AI-first firms, clients, criminal-defense practices, courts, legal-AI vendors and investors.
pts.d:
Individual lawyers: Experienced AI users may accumulate a mindset advantage, while hesitant non-users face a growing adjustment burden. Lawyers can increasingly build custom applications rather than depend exclusively on vendors. Abramowitz does not quantify displacement or predict particular staffing shapes.

Incumbent firms and leaders: Adoption outcomes diverge, training becomes consequential, and leaders face pressure to turn personal assistance into redesigned services. Firms must allocate resources between AI and talent retention while responding to new entrants and better-executing peers.

AI-first firms and departing lawyers: Off-the-shelf AI is described as lowering the resources needed to establish a competing practice. These are legal-service providers, distinct from software vendors such as Harvey.

Clients: The proposed benefits are lower charges, shorter waits and better updates. Abramowitz presents these as objectives firms are working toward, not verified client savings.

Criminal-defense attorneys and courts: He identifies understaffing and shortages of intelligence and reasoning capacity as sources of potential AI demand. The example concerns support for legal work and court functioning; it does not establish that AI has closed an access-to-justice gap.

Legal-AI startups, incumbent vendors and investors: More capable founders and demand for reasoning create opportunities, while lawyer-built alternatives, cheaper development and competition from model providers threaten defensibility and conventional financing assumptions.

Personal-injury firms, AI-first firms and potentially Big Law: External capital may help finance AI alongside talent expenditure. Abramowitz describes personal injury and AI-first firms as existing sites of financing activity and Big Law as an unresolved extension.
